title: Control plane reachability: connectivity sleuth after-action
body:
Summary:

This doc captures the on-call journal and initial after-action for the 2026-04-12 control-plane reachability incidents affecting multiple Private/VPC customers. The outage manifested as intermittent API timeouts to customer control-plane endpoints (10–30s TLS hangs) and a cascade of application-side retries which exhausted ephemeral ports on some on-prem appliance NATs. Impact window ~2026-04-12T05:42–2026-04-12T07:15 UTC.

Symptoms observed (high level):
- Verified increase in TLS handshake latency and TCP retransmits between customer proxies and control-plane hosts.
- Control-plane health checks from customer side reported 503s or connection refused.
- On-prem devices showed conntrack table spikes and NAT exhaustion on a small percentage of customers.
- Platform telemetries: SLO error budget burn for private tenants + multiple alerts from agent heartbeats.

Immediate mitigation applied:
- Rollback of a staging BGP config pushed to two co-located edge routers (rollback initiated at ~05:55 UTC).
- Temporarily increased control-plane ingress capacity by redirecting traffic to a warm standby region for affected customers (manual routing policy change).
- Worked with 2 impacted customers to flush conntrack entries and expand ephemeral port ranges as temporary relief.

Timeline (skeleton):
- 05:42 UTC: First automated agent missing-heartbeat alarms (region-eu-west-2).
- 05:46 UTC: Pager triggered; SRE runbook lookup; initial triage sees elevated TCP retransmits in flow logs.
- 05:52 UTC: SRE on-call attempts graceful drain of one edge host; not effective.
- 05:55 UTC: Correlation with recent router config push (internal change ID: netchg-2026-04-12-91).
- 06:02 UTC: Rollback netchg-2026-04-12-91 on routers A/B. Partial recovery for some tenants.
- 06:20 UTC: Continued TLS handshake spikes traced to packets with DF set being blackholed by a misconfigured inline firewall rule on customer appliance (rule 312).
- 06:40 UTC: Worked with customer infra to remove rule 312; conntrack entries started to drain.
- 07:15 UTC: Metrics returned to baseline; incident declared mitigated.

Root cause hypothesis (final):
A sequence of events produced the outage: a router config push introduced an asymmetric path for certain flows (egress -> control-plane via region-a, return via region-b). That asymmetric routing increased MTU and fragmentation differences; simultaneously, a customer firewall rule (legacy rule 312) dropped fragments or packets with DF flag unexpectedly. The combination caused repeated TLS retransmits, connection stalls, and heavy conntrack creation on the customer NAT causing ephemeral port exhaustion for a subset of sessions.

Evidence and useful snippets (from on-call notes):
- tcpdump sample (edge host):
  05:48:21.123 IP 10.30.5.11.443 > 10.120.1.78.51234: Flags [S], seq 0, win 29200, options [mss 1460], length 0
- conntrack dump (customer appliance immediately before flush):
  # conntrack -L | grep 10.120.1.78
  tcp      6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.120.1.78 dst=10.30.5.11 sport=51234 dport=443 ...
  (thousands of similar entries; table at 97% full)
- iptables rule snapshot (customer):
  -A FORWARD -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
  -A FORWARD -p tcp --dport 443 -m frag --fragid 0 -j DROP  # <-- legacy frag rule (rule 312)

Why this is different from prior incidents:
- Not a single control-plane service crash: the control-plane hosts were responsive but reached via flaky network paths.
- The customer-side firewall had a historical frag-drop rule that only triggered when fragmentation/asymmetry occurred — we rarely see this combination.
- It created a cross-team troubleshooting requirement (SRE + network + customer infra).

Short-term action items (owners + estimate):
- SRE: Add a transient alert for conntrack utilization at tenant boundary (SLA breach predictor) — owner: Priya (2d).
- Neteng: Add validation to router config CI to detect potential asymmetric next-hops across announcements (owner: Diego, 3d).
- Product/Edge: Add a sticky routing policy to prefer symmetric egress for control-plane flows during config rollouts (owner: Samir, 5d).
- Support: Produce a customer-facing KB note explaining how legacy frag rules and NAT conntrack interact; include remediation steps (owner: Maya, 2d).

Longer-term / runbook updates:
- Expand 'control-plane reachability' runbook to include steps for: checking conntrack saturation, identifying legacy fragmentation rules, and a checklist for safe router config rollbacks.
- Add explicit test traffic (fragmented packet sequences) in our staging harness to catch frag-drop behaviours before rollouts.
- Create a post-commit CI gate in netcfg repo that simulates return-path asymmetry for a sample BGP mesh.

Open questions / unresolved items: 
- How many other customers have similar legacy frag rules but are not currently symptomatic? (Support to inventory config templates).
- Can we detect DF-flag drops centrally in flow logs without customer cooperation? (Observability ask).
- Is there a simpler mitigation—e.g., enabling MSS clamping on edge BGP neighbors for affected peers—worth rolling out automatically?

Quick reproduction notes for engineers:
1) Simulate asymmetric path: route client->edge via rtr-A, edge->client via rtr-B; use tc/netem to introduce MTU mismatch.
2) On a firewall appliance, add a rule to drop fragments or packets with DF mismatches.
3) Start TLS flow and watch retransmits from edge tcpdump and conntrack growth on the appliance.

Commands we used during triage: 
- netstat -anp | grep 443
- sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.120.1.78 and port 443 -w /tmp/tcpdump-client.pcap
- sudo conntrack -L | wc -l  # watch for table growth
- iptables-save > /tmp/iptables-pre.txt

Customer communications log (summary):
- 05:58 UTC: Notified customer SEs with initial hypothesis; requested permission for conntrack flush.
- 06:10 UTC: Customer approved temporary conntrack flush and firewall rule adjustment.
- 07:30 UTC: Follow-up call scheduled to walk through permanent mitigations.

Draft text for customer KB (short):
"If your control-plane agents experience intermittent TLS timeouts while other traffic is normal, look for NAT/conntrack saturation and legacy firewall rules that drop fragments or packets with the DF flag. Temporary relief: flush conntrack on the appliance and widen ephemeral port range. Long-term: remove frag-drop rules or enable MSS clamping on edge peering. Contact Redwood Support for help."

Post-incident hygiene checklist (to be completed):
- [ ] Add runbook section and link to this doc (Maya)
- [ ] Create Jira tasks for neteng CI checks (Diego)
- [ ] Rollout MSS-clamp experiment to 10% of customers in staging (Samir)
- [ ] Inventory customer firewall templates for frag rules (Support ops)

Notes to self: keep this doc concise; convert to confluence page after owners triage. Will attach PCAPs and conntrack dumps to the Jira SRE-4821 ticket.

-- end of journal --
